name: The Witch's Spruce

location.address: Rambynas Regional Park, Silute Forest District, Rambynas forestry block 83 plot 53, about 2 km southeast of Vilkyskiai, Pagegiai municipality, Lithuania

access: Free. Stands inside Rambynas Regional Park on managed forest/park land, reached by a raised boardwalk from a signposted roadside parking area (the site is explicitly built to be accessible to visitors with disabilities). No fee or restriction found in either source.
transport: No public transport. By car: from Vilkyskiai take the road toward Sereitlaukis; about 200 m past the town boundary marker (road RK4229) two roadside signs mark 'Lankytina vieta 1.6 km' (point of interest, 1.6 km) and a parking spot 100 m further; from the car park a boardwalk leads roughly 150 m more through forest to the tree.
verify_notes: Multi-stemmed Norway spruce (paprastoji egle), a single trunk that branches into 18 separate stems at about 0.8 m height, which is also where the 5 m girth is measured (an unusual measurement point caused by the branching, not a normal chest-height trunk figure - flag this for the writer). Height 32 m. Age estimated by lt.wikipedia at 160-180 years, no basis given beyond that it is an estimate; treat as a vague sourced estimate, do not sharpen. On 2007-11-10 a storm broke off one of the 18 stems. Declared a Lithuanian nature monument (gamtos paminklas) and named Lithuania's Tree of the Year in 2017 (ve.lt, cited by lt.wikipedia), which qualifies it for the following year's European Tree of the Year contest. TWO LEGENDS worth the story: (1) local folklore says witches gathered at a nearby hillfort (Sidabrakalnis) and used to plant their brooms in this then-small spruce while luring young men, hence the name; (2) a rival legend says Napoleon, retreating from Russia in 1812 in a fury, slashed the treetop with his sword while crossing the Nemunas nearby, and the tree grew its strange multi-stem form from that wound. Specialists quoted by lt.wikipedia think a person deliberately shaped the tree, or that natural damage caused it; either way it is described as the only Norway spruce of this unusual branching form known in Lithuania or Europe. In 1963 naturalist Eugenija Simkunaite visited and joked that since people call her a witch (Ragana), they should give the tree to her when it's felled. COORDINATE NOTE: lt.wikipedia's own infobox gives 55.10414, 22.14302 (about 270 m from the coordinate used here), but the coordinate used here (55.10307, 22.14684) is the GPS geotag baked into the Commons photo File:2018_Witches_Spruce_LT.jpg, i.e. taken standing at the tree, so it is treated as the more reliable of the two and marked confirmed. Environment: soil around the tree was restored with mycorrhizal-fungus-inoculated sawdust and a wide protective fence/zone was built around it (Silute Forest District + Rambynas park authority, reported 2017) to support its vitality, consistent with it still being alive; no report found of it being removed since. Container decision: new single-tree place, prefix rmb (Rambynas), since it stands alone with nothing else mapped nearby and clearly passes the destination test (national Tree of the Year 2017, a purpose-built boardwalk and viewing platform exist specifically for visitors).

name: Perkūnas Oak

location.address: Plunge Manor Park (Oginskiai Park), central part of the park beside the Oginskiai Palace (Samogitian Art Museum), Plunge, Lithuania

access: Free. Stands in the central part of Plunge Manor Park, a public town park (58.3 ha) surrounding the Oginskiai Palace; the palace itself now houses the ticketed Samogitian Art Museum, but the grounds are an open park with a numbered self-guided nature/heritage trail (this tree is stop 10) and a Ciurlionis monument elsewhere in the same park. No fee to walk the park.
transport: In the town of Plunge, Telsiai county, north-west Lithuania; a short walk from the town centre and Plunge railway station (on the Siauliai-Klaipeda line).
verify_notes: The oldest oak of the Plunge Manor park, growing beside the Oginskiai Palace. Declared a nature monument in 1960 and upgraded to nature monument of republican significance in 1987, the oldest protection status of any tree in this park (the other three trees below were only listed in 2016). Girth 4.86 m measured at 0.9 m height (both lt.wikipedia and the official plungesparkas.lt tourist-trail page agree on this figure exactly). Height given as 26 m (both sources agree). Crown diameter about 25 m, leaf cover only about 60%, and lt.wikipedia says the tree has passed natural maturity and is in a 'resignation phase' (declining), with visible lightning-strike scarring on the trunk. No age recorded anywhere; a legend traces the site to a pre-Christian sacred grove (alka) but that is folklore, not a dating basis, so leave age_estimate empty rather than bridge the two. TWO NAMING LEGENDS: (1) a vestal-priestess figure named Galinda wept for a lover who rode off to fight the Teutonic Knights and never returned; while she wept under the oak, the thunder-god Perkunas struck it with lightning, and it has been called Perkunas's oak ever since. (2) after the Christianisation of Samogitia the sacred fire kept at this spot was extinguished, and an angry Perkunas struck the tree in response, giving it the god's name. Local tradition (per lt.wikipedia, sourced to old residents' memories) says Maria Skuzewska, wife of Duke Mykolas Oginskis, staged plays for children under this oak, and a sundial once stood behind it in the Babrungas valley. CONTAINER DECISION: this and the next three entries (plg_002-004) form ONE genuine walkable cluster, all inside Plunge Manor Park, spanning roughly 500-700 m end to end (this oak sits centrally, Aukstasis Oak and Oginskis Linden are about 500 m to the west and 60 m from each other, Laikrodines Oak is about 200-220 m to the southeast of this one). New place: Plunge, prefix plg. This is a much better outcome than four scattered single-tree entries: one park, four state-protected named trees, each independently verifiable.

name: Aukštasis Oak

location.address: Plunge Manor Park, near a small pond in the north-western corner of the park, close to Parko gatve 8, Plunge, Lithuania

access: Free. Stands in the north-western corner of Plunge Manor Park, a public town park, next to a natural path that runs from the Parko gatve street into the park; no fee to walk the park grounds.
transport: In the town of Plunge, Telsiai county, north-west Lithuania; a short walk from the town centre and Plunge railway station.
verify_notes: Named 'the Tall Oak' because it is the tallest tree in Plunge Manor Park. Declared a state-protected botanical natural heritage object in 2016. Two measurement sets disagree slightly, typical of Lithuanian tree records: the official state protected-areas cadastre (via lt.wikipedia) gives 30.5 m height and 4.45 m girth (at 1.3 m); a 2016 State Forest Service survey (cited by lt.wikipedia, amvmt.lrv.lt PDF) gives 33 m height and 4.5 m girth, plus detail that the trunk has a lightning-split, a 4.0x1.0 m cavity on the north-west side, crown fill about 75% with dry branches, and thick dry branches broken off at 8-9 m; the official park tourist-trail page (plungesparkas.lt) gives a third figure, 27.2 m. Recorded girth_cm here (445) uses the state cadastre figure as the most consistently cited; flag the height range (27-33 m depending on source) for the writer rather than picking one. No age documented. Stands about 60 m north of the Mykolo Oginskis Linden (plg_003) and roughly 500 m west of Perkunas Oak (plg_001); part of the same Plunge Manor Park cluster, see plg_001 for the container decision.

name: Mykolas Oginskis Linden

location.address: Plunge Manor Park, western side near Parko gatve 14/16, about 60 m south of the Aukstasis Oak, Plunge, Lithuania

access: Free. Stands on the western side of Plunge Manor Park, a public town park, near a row of private houses on Parko gatve but on park land itself; no fee to walk the park grounds.
transport: In the town of Plunge, Telsiai county, north-west Lithuania; a short walk from the town centre and Plunge railway station.
verify_notes: Named after Duke Mykolas Oginskis, who bought the Plunge estate in 1873 and developed the park around it. A large-leaved lime (Tilia platyphyllos, flowers and sheds leaves earlier than the small-leaved lime). Declared a state-protected botanical natural heritage object in 2016. State cadastre gives 23.6 m height and 4.6 m girth (at 1.3 m); a 2018 State Forest Service survey gives 27 m height and 4.8 m girth with a healthy trunk and very wide healthy crown; the park's own tourist-trail page gives 21.2 m and 4.4 m. Used the state cadastre figures here; flag the height range for the writer. lt.wikipedia describes it as the 'mother' tree of a ring of lime trees planted in the park (4 old limes plus 5 recently planted saplings restoring the pattern), so it is one component of a designed planting rather than a wild survivor. The park's own tourist page adds a folk-symbolism aside, that lime trees traditionally were thought lightning-resistant and were planted as village and homestead guardians, and states lime trees CAN live 500-600 years as a species; this is a general statement about the species' lifespan, not a documented age for this specific tree, so it must not be used as this tree's age (the bridge-claim trap: species longevity is not this specimen's age). No age documented for this individual. Stands about 60 m south of Aukstasis Oak (plg_002) and part of the same Plunge Manor Park cluster, see plg_001 for the container decision.

name: Laikrodinė Oak

location.address: Plunge Manor Park, beside the north facade of the old clock-house/orangery building (now Plunge public library), Parko gatve 7, Plunge, Lithuania

access: Free. Stands beside the former clock-house/orangery building, now Plunge's public library, on the south-eastern side of Plunge Manor Park, a public town park; the tree stands right beside the building's facade on the path side, open ground, no fee.
transport: In the town of Plunge, Telsiai county, north-west Lithuania; a short walk from the town centre and Plunge railway station.
verify_notes: Named for the ornate former clock-house and orangery (laikrodine) it stands beside, now Plunge's public library; estate gardeners used to live in that building and wind the tower clock's stone weights every few days, and when the clock stopped a sundial in the park's flowerbed told the time instead. Declared a state-protected botanical natural heritage object in 2016 as an exceptionally large specimen. State cadastre gives 27.5 m height and 4.7 m girth (at 1.3 m); a 2016 State Forest Service survey gives 30 m height and 4.5 m girth with a lightning-split trunk with a burnt-out crack, branching into 3 stems at 2 m height, crown fill about 80% with pruned lower branches and some dry wood; the park's own tourist page gives 27.4 m and does not restate girth. lt.wikipedia states plainly that the tree is ailing and 'awaiting specialist help' (negaluojantis, laukiantis specialistu pagalbos) and that its main top broke off long ago; still standing and still on the park's own current visitor trail (a 2026-dated photo of it, File:Laikrodines azuolas, 2026.jpg, exists on Commons), so treat as alive but genuinely declining, worth flagging for a future re-check. No age documented. Stands about 200 m south-east of Perkunas Oak (plg_001); part of the same Plunge Manor Park cluster, see plg_001 for the container decision.
